awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I: An Aerogel Wound Dressing Material Platform with Mechanical Fluid Management, Biofilm Prevention, and pH based Infection Detection Properties
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact/commercial potential of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is a novel wound dressing material for improving chronic wound care by mitigating several biological and microbial factors that affect healing. Chronic wounds affect near 50 million patients in developed countries often leading to persistent infections, prolonged inflammation, and increased healthcare costs. Approximately 80% of infections are associated with bacterial biofilms that delay healing and require frequent interventions. Current solutions often rely on reactive infection management and frequent dressing changes.  This project proposes a novel wound dressing with optimal porosity to enable oxygen exchange while creating a pathogen barrier, integrated with real-time detection of infection indicated by a rapid color change. The platform offers a potential solution for improving the management of acute wounds, chronic wounds, surgical sites, and burn, with a total estimated $200M annual market.

This Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project seeks to develop and validate an aerogel-based biomaterial combining fluid management, biofilm prevention, and rapid infection detection properties into a single platform. The innovation relies on the integration of a biopolymer aerogel material with a multi-layer design. The primary layer aims to promote tissue regeneration while blocking microbial infiltration, and the secondary layer aims to absorb wound fluid while providing a visual indicator of infection. The proposed technology development will optimize the aerogel’s pore structure for effective biofilm prevention, refine the infection-sensing mechanism for reliable detection in under a minute, and ensure the mechanical durability needed for clinical use. If successful this project will demonstrate preclinical safety and effectiveness, with scalable pilot production methods for a prototype wound dressing material, that reduces infection-related complications, minimizes dressing changes, and improve healing outcomes.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This NSF SBIR Phase I project focused on developing a new type of wound dressing designed to both support healing and provide a simple, visual indication of wound healing. Chronic and acute wounds remain a significant healthcare challenge, particularly when infection is not identified early. Existing dressings are largely passive and rely on visual inspection or delayed laboratory testing, which can lead to slower intervention and delayed healing. The goal of this project was to address this gap by creating a dressing that can actively respond to changes in the wound environment that indicate healing.

The approach centered on designing a highly porous, lightweight dressing structure that can manage wound fluid while maintaining close contact with the wound surface. The material platform was engineered to provide key properties needed for wound care, including flexibility, conformability, and the ability to maintain a moist environment. Throughout Phase I, multiple design and processing variables were explored to better understand how they influence structural integrity, pore architecture, and overall performance. This work led to the identification of dressing configurations that were consistently stable, easy to handle, and suitable for further biological evaluation.

A central component of the project was the integration of a color-based sensing capability. The dressing was designed to respond to changes in wound pH, which is a well-established indicator of healing progression. Healing wounds tend to be slightly acidic, while non-healing or infected wounds often become more alkaline due to a combination of bacterial activity, inflammation, and tissue breakdown. The developed system translates these changes into a visible color shift, allowing wound status to be assessed quickly without specialized equipment or frequent dressing changes. Testing confirmed that the dressings exhibit clear and reproducible color changes across pH ranges relevant to wound care. The response was consistent and visually distinguishable, particularly under conditions associated with delayed healing or infection. Additional studies showed that environments with higher bacterial activity could induce changes that triggered the color response, supporting the relevance of this approach for real-world wound conditions.

Biological evaluation was also performed to ensure compatibility with wound healing processes. Cell-based studies demonstrated that the dressings support cell attachment and growth, indicating that they can provide a suitable environment for tissue repair. The structure of the material also allowed cells to interact with and integrate into the dressing, which is important for providing a scaffold for tissue regeneration within the wound site. In parallel, testing with common wound-related bacteria showed reduced surface attachment compared to a traditional commercial dressing, suggesting that the material may help limit early stages of bacterial colonization and infection.

Together, these results demonstrate the feasibility of a multifunctional wound dressing that combines structural performance with a simple sensing capability. The project established a clear foundation for further development, including refinement of the sensing response, validation in more complex biological systems, and advancement toward practical use.

From a broader perspective, this work highlights the potential of integrating sensing functionality directly into wound care materials. A dressing that can visually indicate changes in wound condition may help clinicians and patients recognize problems earlier and respond more quickly, enabling earlier intervention. This could improve healing outcomes, reduce complications, and lower overall healthcare costs. The technology also has potential applications beyond wound care in areas where simple, real-time monitoring of biological environments is needed. Future efforts will focus on expanding testing under more realistic conditions, performing validation studies in translational animal models, and advancing the design toward clinical and commercial readiness.
